conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes with a clear 'yes', citing evidence from major randomized controlled trials (such as NLST and NELSON) demonstrating that low-dose CT screening reduces lung cancer mortality in eligible current and former heavy smokers.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion: yes—when “regularly” means following an evidence-based low-dose CT (LDCT) screening program, eligible current and former heavy smokers are less likely to die from lung cancer than comparable people not offered that screening (or offered chest X-ray).** This is evidence from randomized trials, so it is not merely an association.

In the U.S. NLST, 53,454 high-risk current or former heavy smokers were randomized to annual LDCT or chest radiography. LDCT reduced lung-cancer mortality by about 20% relative to chest X-ray.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1102873

The independent Dutch-Belgian NELSON randomized trial compared periodic volume-based LDCT with no screening in high-risk people. At 10 years, the lung-cancer death rate ratio in men was 0.76 (95% CI 0.61–0.94)—about a 24% relative reduction; the trial also reported lower mortality in screened women.  
https://scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl/access/item:3453624/view

The conclusion applies to *high-risk* people, not everyone who has ever smoked. In the U.S., USPSTF recommends annual LDCT for adults 50–80 with at least a 20-pack-year history who currently smoke or quit within 15 years, provided they are healthy enough to benefit from curative treatment.  
https://www.uspreventiveservicestaskforce.org/uspstf/recommendation/lung-cancer-screening

Screening has trade-offs: false-positive or indeterminate findings can lead to repeat scans or invasive tests, and Cochrane estimates CT screening overdiagnosis at about 18%. It complements—not replaces—stopping smoking.  
https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD013829_impact-computed-tomography-ct-lung-cancer-screening
